source_text: interim Marcionites nihil ex huiusmodi exhibebit, cui tum etiam pronuntiare, cuius magis Christus nondum sit reuelatus: sicut meus expectandus est, qui a primordio praedicatus est, illius idcirco non est, quia non a primordio. sic melius nos credimus in Christum futurum quam haereticus in ullum. Mortuorum resurrectionem quomodo quidam tunc negarint, prius dispiciendum est. utique eodem modo quo et nunc; siquidem semper resurrectio carnis negatur. ceterum animam et sapientium plures diuinam uindicantes saluam repromittunt, et uulgus ipsum ea praesumptione defunctos colit, qua animas eorum manere confidit; ceterum corpora aut ignibus statim aut feris aut, etiam diligentissime condita, temporibus tamen aboleri manifestum est. si ergo [carnis] resurrectionem negantes apostolus retundit, utique aduersus illos tuetur quod illi negabant, carnis scilicet resurrectionem. habes compendio responsum. cetera iam ex abundanti.
pass_a_gloss: Meanwhile Marcionites will exhibit nothing of this kind, to whom then also to pronounce, whose Christ has not yet been revealed: just as mine is to be expected, who has been preached from the beginning, that one is not, therefore, because not from the beginning. Thus we believe better in the Christ who is to come than the heretic in any. How some then denied the resurrection of the dead is to be considered first. Certainly in the same way as also now; since indeed the resurrection of the flesh is always denied. Nevertheless, the soul both many of the wise, avenging it as divine, promise it to be saved, and the common people itself, with that presumption, honor the dead, with which it confides that their souls remain; nevertheless, the bodies either to the fires at once or to the beasts or, even having been buried most diligently, are nevertheless abolished by the times. If, therefore, the apostle rebukes those denying the resurrection of the flesh, certainly he defends against those what they were denying, namely the resurrection of the flesh. You have the response in brief. The rest now is from abundance.

choices.english: the rest now is from abundance

pass_b_english: Meanwhile, the Marcionites will show nothing of this sort—people to whom one must now also declare whose Christ has still not been revealed. My Christ is the one to be expected, because he was proclaimed from the beginning; theirs is not, precisely because he was not. So we put our faith in the coming Christ more confidently than the heretic puts his in just any Christ. First we must examine how certain people back then denied the resurrection of the dead. They did it in exactly the same way as they do now, since the resurrection of the flesh has always been denied. Yet many philosophers, claiming the soul is divine, promise its salvation; and the common crowd, relying on that same presumption, honors the dead in the confidence that their souls survive. But everyone can see that bodies are destroyed—thrown straight into fire, devoured by beasts, or even when buried with the utmost care, eventually erased by time. So if the apostle rebukes those who deny the resurrection of the flesh, he is necessarily defending the very thing they denied: the resurrection of the flesh. That is the answer in brief. The rest is simply overkill.

anf_compare.notes: Drafted from source only; ANF not shown to drafter.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances of the source, including the causal relationship in 'illius idcirco non est, quia non a primordio' (theirs is not, precisely because he was not) and the conditional/concessive structure regarding the bodies being abolished by time.
